source.title: The Lexical Imprint of Pre-training Data
source.authors: Jeonghoon Kim; Woo-Jin Chung; Woo-Min Song; Cheonbok Park; Nako Sung; Jin-Woo Shin

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. No apparent truncation or corruption.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses the cited Chinchilla compute-optimal ratio of 20 tokens per parameter to set matched model/data pairings, but does not test power-law loss scaling or compute-optimal allocations.
record.gate_note: The study measures word-level corpus–benchmark unigram cross-entropy (UCE) and downstream benchmark scores, not held-out language-model cross-entropy as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute. It does not fit or evaluate power laws, test small-run extrapolation, or compare compute-optimal allocations. Its reported UCE/accuracy relationships and data-selection effects are related results, but do not measure the variables named by the claim versions. Prompt-routing throughput results are not results about the claim’s loss-scaling subject. Results cited from other papers are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study sets its matched model/token pairings at the Chinchilla ratio of about 20 tokens per parameter (Section 4.1, citing Hoffmann et al.). It never measures held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens or compute, and fits no power law. It does not test extrapolation, compute-optimal splits, shape effects or downstream predictability from scale. Its results concern corpus–benchmark unigram cross-entropy (UCE), UCE-based data selection and drafter routing.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that pre-training corpora leave a measurable lexical imprint on base-model zero-shot behaviour. UCE tracks it at the corpus level, can be controlled via document selection, and can route prompts to drafters. They frame UCE as a lower-bound proxy that is blind to syntax, composition and post-training effects.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies training corpora and document selection, then evaluates downstream benchmark scores and UCE; it does not reproduce a scaling-law loss-sweep or compute-optimal allocation experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by benchmark and corpus: the authors report task-dependent corpus rankings. The UCE-filter gains concentrate on the targeted suite; out-of-target averages stay close to the random control. They report that target choice shifts performance between benchmark groups.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 16 runs of 400M models on 8.5B-token subsets, lower corpus UCE goes with higher zero-shot accuracy (ARC Easy R2=0.928; PIQA R2=0.805).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Corpus–benchmark unigram alignment is associated with downstream zero-shot accuracy across text corpora.

fits_no_version.finding: For 3.36B models trained on 60B tokens, corpus UCE ordering matches the accuracy ordering of C4, DCLM and FineWeb-Edu on all eight benchmarks in Figure 2; the ordering varies by task.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Which corpus gives the best downstream score depends on the benchmark's lexical alignment with the corpus, not on a single corpus-quality ordering.

fits_no_version.finding: Selecting documents for lower UCE against CSR7 raises targeted-suite accuracy over random selection in all four source/scale cells; out-of-target averages stay near random.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Target-aligned document selection shifts zero-shot accuracy toward the targeted benchmarks.

fits_no_version.finding: DSIR's targeted-suite gains over random are smaller than the UCE-filter's, and near zero at 3.33B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Different target-aware selection rules yield different downstream outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: In a 30B Stage-2 case study, a UCE-filtered web subset trained for 200B tokens nearly matches a production mix trained for about 2T tokens (MMLU 74.28 vs 75.61; MMLU-Pro 48.81 vs 48.64).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In this single case, UCE-filtered data matched benchmark scores with about 10x fewer continued-pretraining tokens.

record.problems: The study does not measure the claimed scaling-law outcomes. The authors identify scope limits: UCE is blind to conditional structure, grammar, arithmetic, and non-English benchmarks; selection gains use a known target and are an upper bound rather than unseen-target generalization. The 30B case study uses a single model/mixture operating point and single seed, with inherited Stage 2 hyperparameters and no additional contamination audit beyond production controls.
record.rows_left_out: Not extracted: per-task corpus UCE and benchmark-score entries across Tables 12–18; per-task UCE-filter and five-shot results in Tables 32–34; detailed ablations and robustness tables in Appendices D–G; and prompt-routing throughput results in Table 4. These concern lexical alignment, target-selection behavior, or decoding throughput rather than the loss-scaling variables named by the claim. No claim version is tested.

untested.parts: No sweep of held-out pretraining loss over parameters, tokens or compute; no power-law fit.
No small-run fits extrapolated to larger runs.
The 20 tokens-per-parameter ratio is assumed for configuring runs; no fixed-compute allocation sweep or exponent fit.
No comparison of depth or width at fixed parameter count.
Text-only pretraining; no loss-law test in other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
Accuracy is related to corpus UCE, not to scale or pretraining loss. Larger models score higher incidentally (Tables 13, 2), but no predictive relation is fitted or tested.
No analysis of how exponents or compute-optimal splits depend on setup or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The study contains incidental scale comparisons but does not analyse them as scaling results: 402M vs 1.33B on the same 26B-token subsets (Table 13), and 1.34B vs 3.33B on 70B tokens (Table 2). Larger models score higher on most tasks. These are not loss measurements, and no predictive scaling relation is fitted, so they were not treated as V6 evidence. No row fixes are needed; all rows correctly carry versions ['none']. The Chinchilla ratio is assumed, not tested.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute; no power-law fit.
No predictions from small-run loss fits evaluated on larger runs.
The cited 20-token-per-parameter ratio is used to configure runs; the study does not optimize parameter/token splits at fixed compute or fit their growth exponents.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
Experiments concern text pretraining and text benchmarks; no test of the same loss law in other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The study reports downstream benchmark performance in relation to corpus UCE and data selection, not performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
No analysis of scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits under alternative fitting, counting, data, or schedule choices.
